Body:
I would like something similar to this. Right now there are two main options:

1. Ask to spawn in batches. Models kinda suck at this, they tend to spawns a few at a time, then wait for them all to finish. So your average utilization is only half of the batch size if your tasks are somewhat random in length. Can be much worse depending on the distribution. At the end of the day having the model handle this isn't optimal, it is unreliable and inefficient. Better to let it describe the whole set of tasks and let the framework run them intelligently.
2. Ask to spawn all in parallel. This works pretty well but you get context thrashing due to the current round-robin behaviour. So the model runner constantly needs to unload/reload cached contexts (or recompute the prompt if you run out of cache) which is inefficient. Greatly reducing total throughput.

I think the general concurrent agent limit would be pretty good, it would keep the contexts hot and improve efficiency.

However I think it would be even better if it was more of a priority queue. This way if some of the agents get blocked on other work (not model processing) then more than N agents can run. This way you are always maximizing the use of N local model slots with minimal context and cache thrashing.

So for example if I have a limit of 2, and want to work on a bunch of tests, all of the agents can be spawned in parallel. At first 2 are running in the 2 context slots. However when agent 1 runs a build/test agent 3 can start using the model. Once agent 1 is done then it can get the model back when 2 or 3 starts running tests. Agent 4 will only start if multiple of the first 3 are building/running at the same time, later agents are unlikely to start running at all until one of the earlier one finishes.

So basically I am suggesting that in most cases a soft concurrency limit implemented by a priority system (rather than the current effective round-robin) may be better in most cases. Having a hard concurrency limit may also be useful as a fallback (if every agent starts running tests at the same time it may not be very helpful to start agent \#20) but for me the soft limit would be the main mechanism as it would greatly improve efficiency.

Confirmed deterministic reproduction + root cause + a minimal patch below. This is the same bug as #29209 viewed from the parent agent's side (parent sees `completed` with empty output; the child DB row shows the actual `Tool execution aborted` truth).

## Indicator chain (5/5 match)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `part.tool` | `bash` (or whatever streaming tool was in flight) |
| `part.state.status` | `error` |
| `part.state.error` | `"Tool execution aborted"` |
| `part.state.input` | `{}`  ← **payload lost** |
| `part.metadata.interrupted` | `true` |
| `message.finish` | `"unknown"` |
| `message.tokens.total` | `0` |

If you query `opencode.db` after a "completed-but-empty" subagent return, you will find a row matching all five fields.

## Root cause — `packages/opencode/src/session/processor.ts:892-924`

Two issues compound in the cleanup path on session abort:

**(a)** The grace timeout for in-flight tool calls is hardcoded at 250 ms:

```ts
yield* Effect.forEach(
  Object.values(ctx.toolcalls),
  (call) => Deferred.await(call.done).pipe(Effect.timeout("250 millis"), Effect.ignore),
  { concurrency: "unbounded" },
)
```

That window was tuned for completed-tool execution races. For reasoning models like `gpt-5.5` that emit multi-kilobyte tool arguments via SSE deltas, the streaming window is routinely **tens of seconds**, so the timeout always trips.

**(b)** Once the timeout trips, the cleanup discards `ctx.toolcalls[id].raw` (the accumulated streaming bytes) and writes the part with `state.input = {}`:

```ts
yield* session.updatePart({
  ...part,
  state: {
    ...part.state,
    status: "error",
    error: "Tool execution aborted",
    metadata: { ...metadata, interrupted: true },
    time: { start: ..., end },
  },
})
```

The streamed `raw` never makes it to disk, so parent agents and downstream tooling can't reconstruct what the model was about to invoke — which is exactly the "completed but empty" symptom this issue describes.

## Deterministic repro (no source patches needed)

1. Launch a background subagent that asks `gpt-5.5` (or any reasoning model with slow tool-args streaming) to emit **one** bash tool call with a `command` argument 4000+ characters long. Suggested prompt: "emit one bash one-liner that runs a complex `jq` filter against every `.ts` file under `packages/opencode/src`; the jq filter must reference every field explicitly; no temp files, no heredoc, no splitting."
2. Wait ~30–40s while the model finishes reasoning and starts streaming the tool-input deltas.
3. Cancel the subagent (Esc Esc / `background_cancel` / parent abort).
4. Inspect the child session's last `tool` part in `opencode.db`. You will see the 5-field indicator chain above.

I just ran this with a 35-second wait and a single `background_cancel` call — the indicator chain reproduced exactly, with `state.input = {}` and a streamed `raw` payload silently dropped by cleanup.

## Suggested fix (minimal, schema-compatible)

Two changes, both isolated to `processor.ts`:

```diff
+const SALVAGE_RAW_MAX = 4096
+
+function salvageStreamingToolInput(
+  raw: string | undefined,
+  fallback: Record<string, any>,
+): { input: Record<string, any>; rawSnapshot?: string } {
+  if (!raw) return { input: fallback }
+  try {
+    const parsed = JSON.parse(raw)
+    if (isRecord(parsed)) return { input: parsed }
+  } catch {
+    // streaming was interrupted mid-token; fall through to raw snapshot
+  }
+  return {
+    input: fallback,
+    rawSnapshot: raw.length > SALVAGE_RAW_MAX ? raw.slice(0, SALVAGE_RAW_MAX) + "…[truncated]" : raw,
+  }
+}
```

```diff
-  (call) => Deferred.await(call.done).pipe(Effect.timeout("250 millis"), Effect.ignore),
+  (call) => Deferred.await(call.done).pipe(Effect.timeout("1500 millis"), Effect.ignore),
```

```diff
   const metadata = "metadata" in part.state && isRecord(part.state.metadata) ? part.state.metadata : {}
+  const fallbackInput = "input" in part.state && isRecord(part.state.input) ? part.state.input : {}
+

Hi @ReStranger, thanks for the fix. One issue: this only fixes the `opencode` derivation, not `opencode-desktop`.

The PR adds the Bun version-check workaround in `nix/opencode.nix` via `postPatch`, but `nix/desktop.nix` defines its own derivation and its own `postPatch`. It inherits `version`, `src`, `node_modules`, and `patches` from `opencode`, but it does not inherit or run `opencode.postPatch`.

As a result, `opencode-desktop` still builds with the unmodified `packages/script/src/index.ts` and fails during `bun ./scripts/prebuild.ts` with:

```text
This script requires bun@^1.3.14, but you are using bun@1.3.13
```

A fix would need to either move this workaround into a shared `patches` entry inherited by `desktop.nix`, or apply the same `substituteInPlace packages/script/src/index.ts` in `nix/desktop.nix.postPatch` as well.

@rekram1-node the initial issue is resolved, but I'd like to leave this open to request better logging support and better error messages, so that the log file is not empty when we get an error like this.

I've captured heap snapshots following the Memory Megathread instructions (manual Ctrl+P flow).

**Files generated:**
- `server.heapsnapshot` (100 MB)
- `tui.heapsnapshot` (58 MB)

**Heap analysis summary:**

| Metric | server | tui |
|--------|--------|-----|
| Total nodes | 1,670,688 | 916,586 |
| Self size | 154.7 MB | 99.4 MB |
| Objects | 924k | 342k |
| Closures | 388k | 246k |
| Strings | 90k | 106k |

**Notable findings:**
- **2.6M total objects** across both processes — each GC mark-sweep cycle must traverse this entire graph
- **634k closures** — closures retain enclosing scope references, a common leak source
- **33.5 MB ArrayBuffer** — single large buffer potentially leaked
- **Duplicate system prompts** — same prompt strings stored multiple times (15-32 KB each)
- **Multiple 500KB+ WeakMaps** — large key-value stores not being released

This directly explains the CPU spikes: the massive object graph (2.6M nodes) means V8's concurrent GC threads are constantly working even when idle, and each GC pause grows longer as the heap accumulates.

Will upload the snapshots to the Dropbox link shortly (network restrictions on my end). Let me know if there's an alternative upload method available.

**Reproduced on native hardware — official `1.17.9`, Bun's own panic.** Answering your five questions:

### 1. Exact opencode commit / version tested
- **Official `opencode 1.17.9`** (the released `opencode-linux-arm64` binary — *not* my fork). The crash below is from it.
- Bun: **`v1.3.14 (0d9b296a)`**, Linux arm64, kernel `6.17.0`, glibc `2.39`.
- Deps as before: `web-tree-sitter@0.25.10`, `tree-sitter-bash@0.25.0`.

### 2. Full raw crash output (Bun signature + fault address)
Captured live during a real agent run (`opencode run --agent plan --dir <repo>`):

```
============================================================
Bun v1.3.14 (0d9b296a) Linux arm64
Linux Kernel v6.17.0 | glibc v2.39
CPU: neon fp aes crc32 atomics sve
Args: ".../opencode" "--user-agent=opencode/1.17.9" "--use-system-ca" "--" "run" "--agent" "plan" "--dir" ...
Elapsed: 123843ms | User: 21809ms | Sys: 2748ms
RSS: 69.93MB | Peak: 0.64GB | Commit: 69.93MB | Faults: 1

panic: Segmentation fault at address 0xEA8E00000012
oh no: Bun has crashed. This indicates a bug in Bun, not your code.

https://bun.report/1.3.14/La10d9b296mgGugogCmw2wqE+lFmmu9yEmmu9yEujxt/E+5kjgFuvz/8E+1/wqE21shB2096BA28o1DkB
```

The `bun.report` link carries the symbolicated stack for the Bun team.

**Fault-address pattern (important):** an earlier capture on this box faulted at **`0xE3C500000012`**; this one at **`0xEA8E00000012`**. Both end in **`…00000012`** — identical low 32 bits (offset `0x12`), only the high 16 bits differ (ASLR-varied). Two independent crashes with the same field offset → a **consistent tagged-pointer / NaN-box corruption in JSC**, dereferencing a corrupted JSValue at `+0x12`. Not random memory.

### 3. Does the minimal standalone script crash on this hardware?
**No.** I ran your exact script natively on the GB10 plus escalations — none crash:
- your script verbatim → OK
- 200,000-iteration `parse` loop (force JSC Wasm tier-up) → OK
- 8 concurrent workers × 40,000 iters, each a full cursor walk (`gotoFirstChild`/`namedChildren`/`.text`) + GC pressure → OK
- all of the above compiled with `bun build --compile` → OK

So `Parser.init()` + parse in isolation is **not** sufficient. The crash only manifests inside the **full opencode runtime**, intermittently (it took many real agent sessions to fire one), and — notably — this capture crashed in the **plan agent while doing file `Read`s of a large source file**, *not* in the shell-tool WASM init. So this is a **broader JSC corruption**, not specific to `web-tree-sitter` (which only happened to be one trigger). My `shell.ts` guard sidesteps one path; the underlying JSC bug is wider.

### 4. v1.17.9 / v1.17.11 / dev
- **v1.17.9 (official): crashes** (above).
- Same `shell.ts` blob across versions per your check; the bug is in **Bun/JSC**, not opencode source, so version-to-version opencode diffs aren't the variable.

### 5. `BUN_JSC_useWasmIPInt=0`
No observable change — but inconclusive, since I can't trigger the crash deterministically in isolation to A/B it, and this capture wasn't in the Wasm interpreter path anyway.

---

### The likely missing variable: **SVE / Neoverse-V2**
Note the crash report's `CPU: neon fp aes crc32 atomics **sve**`. This is an **NVIDIA GB10 (Grace, ARM Neoverse-V2)** with **SVE (Scalable Vector Extension)**. Your QEMU CPU models (`max`, `cortex-a76`, `neoverse-n1`) **do not implement Neoverse-V2 / SVE** the way real V2 silicon does — that's very likely why QEMU never reproduced. Recommend testing on real Grace/GH200/GB10, or QEMU `-cpu neoverse-v2,sve=on`.

**Summary for the Bun team:** intermittent JSC tagged-pointer corruption (fault always `…+0x12`) under sustained real workload on Neoverse-V2 + SVE + Bun 1.3.14, reproducible in official opencode 1.17.9. `bun.report` link above has the stack.
